newsitem.title: USA: Canada boasts lower business costs than U.S.- study.
newsitem.headline: Canada boasts lower business costs than U.S.- study.

text.p: Business operating costs, particularly labor costs, are significantly lower in Canada than in the U.S., Canadian consulting firm KPMG reported in a study of 23 Canadian and American cities released on Tuesday.

The study "shows that cities right across Canada are excellent sites for investment by U.S. firms," said Art Eggleton, Canadian Minister for International Trade. "Canada is a very competitive place in which to locate."
"The image of Canada as having higher labor costs is simply not accurate," said Stuart MacKay, partner in KPMG's Vancouver office and director of the study.
"When all the costs of U.S. labor are factored in and converted to Canadian dollars, the net advantage to Canada is significant," MacKay said.
For every industry examined, overall costs are lower in Canada than in the U.S., according to the study.

Business costs related to location are, on average, 15.7 percent lower in Canada, the study showed. These costs amount to about 40 percent of total operating costs and lead to an after-tax cost advantage of 6.7 percent.
The size of the Canadian advantage varies by industry, ranging from 5.5 percent for telecommunications to 10.5 percent for software production, according to the study.
Industrial land, construction and electricity costs are also lower in Canada, it said. Income-tax credits for research and development currently favor Canadian locations.

Even the largest Canadian centers are less costly than all of the U.S. locations examined, and Canada's overall cost advantage remains as long as the Canadian dollar exchange rate is under US$0.87, the study said.
The study compared the costs of establishing and operating industrial facilities across seven industries in suburban cites in 13 Canadian and 10 U.S. jurisdictions.
KPMG developed a computer-based model to compare start-up and operating costs for 10 years of operation, assuming comparable sales and distribution patterns for each location.
Each company was assumed to have sales of more than $10 million and a minimum of 100 employees.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade, the Royal Bank of Canada and the Economic Developers Association of Canada sponsored the study called "The Competitive Alternative: A Comparison of Business Costs in Canada and the United States."
